https://archive.nytimes.com/lens.blogs.n.text: Lens: Photography, Video and Visual Journalism Follow Lens: Facebook Twitter RSS Slide Show View Slide Show 17 Photographs Behind the Iron Curtain: Intimate Views of Life in Communist Hungary Behind the Iron Curtain: Intimate Views of Life in Communist Hungary Credit Andras Bankuti Supported by Featured Posts Slide Show View Slide Show 21 Photographs A Father, a Son, a Disease and a Camera A Father, a Son, a Disease and a Camera Credit Cheney Orr Slide Show View Slide Show 12 Photographs Roger Fenton: The First Great War Photographer Roger Fenton: The First Great War Photographer Credit Roger Fenton/Royal Collection Trust/HM Queen Elizabeth II 2017 Slide Show View Slide Show 22 Photographs A Photographer Captures His Community in a Changing Chicago Barrio A Photographer Captures His Community in a Changing Chicago Barrio Credit Sebastián Hidalgo Slide Show View Slide Show 10 Photographs What Martin Luther King Jr. Meant to New York What Martin Luther King Jr. Meant to New York Credit Courtesy of Steven Kasher Gallery Slide Show View Slide Show 12 Photographs Exploring the History of Afro-Mexicans Exploring the History of Afro-Mexicans Credit Mara Sanchez Renero Slide Show View Slide Show 17 Photographs Behind the Iron Curtain: Intimate Views of Life in Communist Hungary Behind the Iron Curtain: Intimate Views of Life in Communist Hungary Credit Andras Bankuti Slide Show View Slide Show 17 Photographs Behind the Iron Curtain: Intimate Views of Life in Communist Hungary Behind the Iron Curtain: Intimate Views of Life in Communist Hungary Credit Andras Bankuti Photographing in socialist Hungary in the decades leading to democratic rule, Andras Bankuti knew that everything was political. Aware of taboo subjects – religion, poverty, drugs, among others – he resorted to self-censorship. “The second I pressed the shutter release,” he said, “I knew which of my pictures could not be published.” Hungary was ruled as a socialist republic from 1949 until 1989, when activists and intellectuals pressed the government to adopt a democratic political system with a revised constitution that affirmed civil rights. Mr. Bankuti’s images from the 1980s and 1990s straddle this complex period, and include intimate depictions of struggling families — people sleeping in the streets, piled together on a bed — as well as celebratory christenings and rousing political gatherings. And even as the state loosened its grip, he had to be careful about his audience. “All the conscientious reporters worked for their own archives,” he said. “The negatives got stored away in drawers, maybe shown to small professional audiences in exhibition rooms tucked away in nameless alleyways.” Photo Homeless people sleeping at Keleti Railway Station in Budapest, Hungary. 1989. Credit Andras Bankuti Mr. Bankuti was born into a bilingual family: His Russian-born mother took him to museums, and his Hungarian-born father was a radio reporter whom he accompanied to interviews. When a long hospitalization toward the end of high school forced him to miss preparations for university entrance exams, he decided to enroll in a vocational school for photography. He continued working in the photo departments of various publications, and for 16 years, he was both a photographer and the head of the photography department for HVG, an economics weekly. Along with Karoly Kincses and Magdolna Kolta, Mr. Bankuti founded the Hungarian Photographers House ( Mai Manó House ). His work from that era had a wide range. He photographed the fringe Hungarian punk scene, earning invitations to house parties and concerts, and his right to take photographs by paying for drinks. He has been taking pictures of the Ballet of Gyor since the company was founded in 1979, covering generations of dancers onstage and backstage, through lyrical moments and physical hardships. He portrayed precarious reality not only in Hungary, but also in neighboring countries, including the demolition of the Berlin Wall, the civil war in Yugoslavia and the fall of the Soviet Union. “I think I had an eye for the changes,” he said. “A good picture is a good picture everywhere, and with the right caption you can make the circumstances understandable even to those in different countries.” Throughout, he was guided by the desire to get close to his subjects. “I have to approach my subjects so that they feel my empathy, and reward me with their trust,” Mr. Bankuti said. “You can detect if either of these is lacking in a picture.” Photo Maria Mikula’s first communion dress. Nagybaracska, Hungary. 1985. Credit Andras Bankuti Gaining that trust was difficult when he started working for the press 40 years ago, an era when socialism seemed undefeatable and politics permeated every aspect of life. “Even professional developments had shades of the political,” he said. “If certain changes seemed uncomfortable for the leadership, the initiator of the reform was soon proclaimed a traitor, an enemy of communism. This was especially true for the press.” During the ’80s, reporting on poverty, Romani, religion or employment difficulties was forbidden. “According to the media, no drugs, prostitution, or pollution existed in Hungary,” he noted. “In such circumstances, we all had self-censorship; people knew exactly what could be published or not, and what to try to slip through to photo competitions.” He recalled “investigations on cooked-up charges against me,” as well as when the head of the newly founded Hungarian stock exchange insinuated that a photo of his, depicting Transylvanian refugees sleeping at a railway station in Budapest, was “degrading the country.” Even the Hungarian Press Photo Competition provided an alternative outlet only in theory. When images he made of Pope John Paul II — that his editor discouraged him from even taking — were selected for exhibition, censors took them off the walls. Other images at the same exhibition were removed: one showing Russian foreign minister Andrei Gromyko in a hunting cap, rather than a hat; another showing nude extras on a film set. Restrictions loosened after 1988, although “the extent still depended on the individual editors’ courage, as criticism still posed an existential threat.” He recounted the risk of photographing an ailing Janos Kadar, the Hungarian communist leader and the General Secretary of the Hungarian Socialist Workers’ Party, who presided over the country from 1956 until 1988. “I took it at a public event, but still I had to look around to see if I was being watched by the state news agency’s employees. I could have easily been arrested. I took the picture because you could already sense, from his speeches, that he was on his way down,” Mr. Bankuti said. “I wanted to picture this state. Today it is an emblematic picture of the end of his regime.” Correction: January 10, 2018 An earlier version of a picture caption with this article misidentified one of the subjects in the photograph. He is Sandor Gaspar, president of the Hungarian National Council of Trade Unions, not the Hungarian actor of the same name. Follow @ nytimesphoto on Twitter. You can also find Lens on Facebook and Instagram . Everything from gallons of hazardous wastewater spills to elevated gas well temps. In a sign of transparency, the landfill opened its doors to one of our crews, while also giving residents a tour of its operations. 21 News reporter Corey McCrae got a first hand look at how the company is taking corrective actions in the wake of recent violations. On any given day you'll see hundreds of customers taking waste into the Republic Services-owned Carbon Limestone Landfill in Poland Township. Every ton of waste has to be monitored and recorded. “We are strictly municipal solid waste, industrial and commercial wastes that are nonhazardous. They go through a profiling process and approval process through the company,” said Mark Jobe, general manager at the Republic Services-owned facility. Each area where trash will be buried is planned out a year in advance. In that time, protective liners and layers are put in place to protect the soil and groundwater beneath it. All the while leachate, the byproduct of rainwater filtering through trash, can create hazardous waste. Leachate is collected, stored, and treated. “Some times in those processes, mother nature can become a little bit more than what a site can handle, given the amount of monitoring that you do have in place.” Jobe explained. Excessive rain at the landfill this year has led to six Ohio EPA violations since June for unintentional leachate discharge. In every instance it was reported to the EPA. Prior, it's been a clean bill back to 2024. “We have put several things into place since then, we have added additional monitoring to our leachate collection systems that now will text myself and our operations team when levels reach a certain limit. We can then act immediately,” said Jobe. Jobe says the many monitored gas wells serve to trap trash gas before the smells can escape. Recent gas temperature exceedances are being tended to with solutions that often involve adding more soil, or replacing the gas wells altogether. People living nearby also got to see operations first hand. “You worry about the water seepage you know, but then you see how thick the liners are and how well they take care of this place, and there is no concerns, I don’t have any, anyhow,” said John Augustine, a Poland resident. After recent leaks, the Mahoning County Health Department tested nearby residential wells. The results of those tests are anticipated to be compiled next week. (AP Photo/Michael Probst, File) (AP Photo/Michael Probst) ELSENBORN, Belgium (AP) — The wildfires burning across Europe this summer have exposed a potentially deadly threat lurking beneath the blackened landscape: rusty bombs and mines from World War I and II that threaten crews responding to the flames. Some of the weapons have exploded in the intense heat. Blasts have been reported in France, Belgium, Germany and the Netherlands, where a bomb-disposal team was dispatched to check a forest threatened by flames near a site of fierce fighting in the Limburg province in 1944. Fueled by climate change, the fires and explosions show that the continent's "climatic luck" is running out, said Sarah Njeri, a peace and conflict scholar at London's School of Oriental and African Studies. Steady temperatures and predictable rainfall once ensured that most buried weapons stayed dormant. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "Climate change is now doing the work of unburying and reactivating what was previously stable," Njeri said. Fires can ignite old munitions but can also burn away the scrub and brush that hides them. This wildfire season was supercharged by heavy rains in January that spurred vegetation growth, which became kindling when the summer heat arrived. Those temperatures, combined with drought conditions, low humidity and stiff winds, offered an ideal environment for fire, according to a study issued last month by the World Weather Attribution group. Flames chewed up old battlefields and set off buried explosives As they advanced, the flames moved over territory that has long been known to hold unexploded weapons, a lethal legacy that lingered long after the guns fell silent. In a forest in tinder-dry France, a massive wildfire outside the southwestern city of Bordeaux uncovered a cache of what is believed to be World War II-era ammunition. Advertisement Advertisement In the eastern Belgian province of Liege, Gov. Hervé Jamar said "a few sporadic detonations" were recently heard and that emergency services were adapting to account for munitions buried in a fire area. He said no fire crews were in danger, but local media published photos of a firefighter handling a rusted bomb. During World War II, booby traps, bombs and mines were sprinkled throughout the province's dense peat-bog forest known as the High Fens. In the first four years after Germany's surrender in 1945, the munitions killed six civilians, said Bernard Collard, a local historian who runs the Truschbaum Museum near Belgium's border with Germany that houses a collection of found objects from the war. "When you go into a forest like this, you are not sure where the explosives are," he said. He remembers his father detonating a found bomb in a quarry. The fire in the High Fens, which stretches across the border with Germany, is smoldering atop a much-bloodied battlefield where Nazis fought Allied troops. The Battle of the Bulge was fought in and around the High Fens. Advertisement Advertisement The fire is even closer to the sites of two lesser-known skirmishes along Elsenborn Ridge and in the Hurtgen Forest, which lasted 88 days and killed about 33,000 American and 28,000 German troops. Every year, Belgium responds to thousands of calls about explosives Collard is authorized to scan with a metal detector the former battlefields, now forests, pastures and farmland. He has found mortar shells, machine guns, helmets, cigarette cases, and once, a human skeleton. "You never know what you might come across, and you shouldn't take it lightly," Collard said while standing in a field that was once a blood-soaked site. Nearby, blueberry bushes cover old foxholes, trenches and deep craters from artillery fire. He frequently works with the Belgian demining squad. "It's part of our history. We live with it," Collard said. Advertisement Advertisement Unexploded ordnance is even more dangerous around wildfires because heat can trigger the explosives, said Jonas Tepe, a spokesperson for North Rhine-Westphalia, just across the border in Germany. The Belgian Ministry of Defense said it receives requests from the region about every week to assist in disarming explosives, yet it does not consider the area a "hot spot" compared to elsewhere in Belgium. Such requests are even more common in the west, where farmers in towns such as Ypres — infamous for harrowing trench warfare in World War I — call the annual tilling of the soil " the iron harvest " because it turns up so many war remnants. Every year across the nation, Belgium's Explosive Ordnance Disposal and Destruction Service responds to more than 3,000 calls and disposes of 200 to 250 tons of munitions left over from both world wars. Flames are not the only threat Drought has also helped to lay the past bare by shrinking rivers and lakes to reveal old weapons. Advertisement Advertisement In Slovakia, the Danube River fell and exposed two naval mines that police pulled out of the water and buried in a trench for a controlled demolition. Authorities in Hungary closed Budapest's Margaret Bridge after a bomb dating from World War II emerged at its base in receding water. As the Rhine dried up, German authorities also found a WWII-era bomb . Christina Greene, a researcher at the University of Arizona who, with Njeri, wrote an article on Europe's wildfires and unexploded ordnance risk, said "the legacy of war keeps creeping up" because of climate change. "It's reliving the legacies of war and conflict in a way that we haven't had to deal with in a while in certain places." Advertisement Advertisement ___ Associated Press writers Mike Corder in The Hague, Netherlands; Sylvain Plazy in Brussels; Angela Charlton in Paris; Kirsten Grieshaber in Berlin; and Stanislav Hodina in Prague contributed to this report. https://telex.hu/english/2026/09/07/mini.text: Menü Kereső Hungarian Ministry of Foreign Affairs bought rapid tests at triple the price during COVID-19 pandemic, memo says English Pál Tamás Andrea Horváth Kávai (translation) Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom According to a memo drafted at the Hungarian Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade during the Covid-19 pandemic, coronavirus tests had been purchased from an intermediary company at triple the price, 444 reports. “It is up to management to decide whether to pursue negotiations with the company about the $384,000 ‘profit’ realized during the procurement (67.37 percent of the total purchase price), since it resold the products to us at triple the price”-the newly discovered document, written at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs states, referring to Speciál 99 Külkereskedelmi Kft., which purchased 30,000 rapid tests in China during the first year of the coronavirus pandemic, in earls 2020. Speciál 99 Kft. purchased the tests for a total of $186,000 and then sold them to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs for $570,000. In other words, they made nearly $13 on each test sold, resulting in a profit of nearly $384,000, which amounted to more than 115 million forints at the time. The memo, written during Péter Szijjártó’s tenure as minister, was titled “Background material on issues concerning companies that invoice certain products at different prices.” It bears no signature or date, but according to 444, it was likely drafted in late 2020, and there is no indication that any action was taken later to recover the difference. According to the publication, the document was discovered after the change in government, during a thorough review of the ministry. The background document also mentions several other companies from which the ministry purchased COVID-19 tests. Specifically, it details purchases from TMT Technics, Pro Concept, OTT-ONE, the Gyömrői-sarok Project, and Marosport, with a note for each stating that it is up to the leadership to decide whether to “discuss profits” with each company. György László Velkey, Parliamentary State Secretary of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs previously wrote on his Facebook page that these six companies alone realized at least 15.5 billion forints (€ 42.78 million) in profit. 444 notes that far more companies were involved in pandemic-related procurements than are mentioned in the background document, which has now been made public. The paper contacted the companies listed in the memo but received no response from any of them. https://www.hindustantimes.com/world-new.text: Poland's Constitutional Tribunal president Bogdan Swieczkowski was removed by the court's longest-serving judge, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, on Friday. This sparked unrest ahead of the parliamentary elections slated to take place in 2027.Polish President Karol Nawrocki was enroute Senegal but turned his plane around after his far-right ally was suspended for a year, escalating the row with pro-EU Prime Minister Donald Tusk and his government for control of the judiciary.Swieczkowski had been appointed by Tusk's far-right predecessor and after news of his suspension broke, hundreds of protesters gathered outside the tribunal. Right-wing politicians reportedly addressed the crowd and accused the Tusk government of carrying out a coup against the court. Also Read | Poland opposition accuses Tusk government of 'coup' as police surround top court Riot police were deployed to control the crowds. Heavy police presence was seen around the courthouse as cops tried to prevent protesters from entering. Three attempting to get into the premises were reportedly arrested. Long-running conflict over court sees new dramaThe crisis over the Constitutional Tribunal has been carrying on since 2015. It has effectively paralysed the institution, Reuters noted, as the pro-European government and the nationalist president have refused to recognise candidates put forth by either side. The dispute began with the nationalist Law and Justice seeking to appoint judges to seats already held by the previous government. While the nominees gained a majority on the Constitutional Tribunal, The European Union’s top court ruled in 2021 that the tribunal is not independent and impartial in its rulings.The Constitutional Tribunal is Poland's highest constitutional court. Its main job is deciding if laws passed by parliament and other state actions comply with the nation's constitution. Both sides have been vying for control over this court as it serves as the ultimate gatekeeper for the nation's laws and government policies. How Tusk and Nawrocki escalated mattersTusk's coalition took office in 2023 and made the pledge to restore the rule of law, and reform the court. However, when Nawrocki was elected president in 2025, the Law and Justice ally acted to thwart said efforts. Friday's escalation saw Law and Justice party (PiS) protesting Swieczkowski's ouster. Earlier in 2026, Nawrocki had refused to swear in three of six judges that the parliament nominated. Swieczkowski, a former deputy justice minister in the Law and Justice administration, did not seat judges elected by the current parliamentary majority. Meanwhile, in September, the parliament appointed Tusk's ally Maciej Berek to the tribunal, which critics said was undermining the government's goal of restoring checks and balances.What key figures have said about the ongoing crisisNawrocki, while returning to Poland, stressed on the urgency of the situation and said, “At a moment like this, the President must be in Poland. I am cutting short my flight to Senegal. I am returning.” Tusk, justifying the events of the day, wrote on X, “Restoring the rule of law is our duty. After years of PiS-led lawlessness, this is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way.” Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said, “The constitutional tribunal was politicized under the previous government. What is happening has the purpose of allowing the majority of duly elected judges to make the tribunal function again,” speaking to reporters on the sidelines of the G20 meeting in Atlanta. Law and Justice party leader Jaroslaw Kaczynski, who has been protesting for weeks in anticipation of this move remarked, “This is the first case of its kind in the world. Starting today, Poland is becoming a police state, and from there it’s a straight path to authoritarianism.” (With agency inputs)
